rationale: B wins because it keeps the story inside the evidence instead of decorating the launch with borrowed drama. Its "Flat fee vs. interchange: the math behind Plaid's \"up to 70% cheaper\" claim" is exactly the right reporter-shaped test: useful, bounded, and honest about what must be proven. A has more ambition, but "FedNow just got its most significant commercial test" is an unearned superlative, and "competing simultaneously with Stripe and Adyen" imports a competitive frame the update did not give it.
gaps_in_A: "FedNow just got its most significant commercial test" overclaims. The update says Pay by Bank uses FedNow rails; it does not prove this is FedNow's biggest commercial test.
"competing simultaneously with Stripe and Adyen" is outside the supplied facts. Maybe true in the market, but the model was asked to work from this update, not its payments-industry memory.
"Plaid spent a decade building the data pipes" drags in company-history color that was not provided. The angle can be saved, but the proof burden needs to be stated instead of assumed.
"network density is what makes this different from prior A2A attempts" is a thesis, not a grounded fact. It needs evidence on prior A2A failures and Plaid's actual merchant reach.
gaps_in_B: It misses the plausible Plaid-strategy angle: the move from bank-data connectivity into payments. A cautious version of that would help a fintech-strategy reporter.

"The other kept angles zoom up to the FedNow rails and down to the fee math" undersells the overlap between the interchange angle and the fee-math angle; those are adjacent, not fully separate planets.
"this is an early merchant-payments use of them" is reasonable but still asserted from "new FedNow rails" rather than evidenced with FedNow adoption context.
The uncomfortable questions skip the ACH baseline. A reporter will ask how the flat fee compares with ACH or same-day ACH, not only card interchange.
